newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich may have broken promise with call - report.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich may have broken promise with call - report.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich may have broken a promise he made to an ethics subcommittee when he had a telephone conference call with other Republicans to discuss tactics just before ethics charges against him were made public, the New York Times reported Friday.

The newspaper said the call was recorded by people in Florida who were unsympathetic to Gingrich. They gave a tape to a Democratic congressman, who made a transcript available to the New York Times. The call was apparently heard on a police scanner radio that picked up the cellular telephone signals of one of the participants.

On the day last month when Gingrich admitted bringing discredit on the House of Representatives, his lawyer told Republican leaders the Speaker had promised the subcommittee not to orchestrate a counter-attack against the charges, the newspaper said.

But it said on that day, Dec. 21 -- before the charges were made public -- Gingrich and Republican allies discussed how to handle Democratic attacks, the timing of the day's events for television, newspapers and news agencies and how to avoid making it look like Gingrich was behind the campaign.

Gingrich admitted on Dec. 21 he had failed to get legal advice to ensure compliance with a ban on using tax-exempt funds for partisan political activity and had given false information to investigators. He was narrowly re-elected House Speaker on Tuesday, with nine Republicans refusing to vote for him because of his admitted ethics violations.

The New York Times reported that the voices of Gingrich and other Republican leaders were recognisable on the tape and that the conversation took place before the subcommittee released its charges and Gingrich's admissions.

Ed Bethune, the attorney who conveyed the Speaker's promise to the subcommittee, is heard saying, "If I could strongly make this one point. It is very important for me to be able to say to the special counsel and if necessary to the committee members that we -- and by that I mean the other attorney Randy Evans, and I, and Newt -- have done everything in our power to to try to stop all things that might be construed in any way as an orchestration attempt by Newt Gingrich."
The New York Times quoted a spokeswoman for Gingrich as defending the Speaker's role.

"There was a specific agreement between Newt's lawyers and the special counsel that Newt could brief the leadership. And it was always understood that in turn, the leadership could respond in any way they thought was appropriate."

In the recorded telephone call, Bethune said that within hours, when the subcommittee announced the charges, "it would also be a time when we are authorised to have the conversation we are having now, a little prematurely. But I don't think it would be troubling anyone that we are a little ahead of the gun."
On Thursday night, Republicans on the House Ethics Committee bowed to Democrats' protests and abruptly changed plans for hearings on the ethics charges against Gingrich.

Democrats had complained the House was being asked to vote on Jan. 21 on a punishment for Gingrich's admitted ethics violations before the committee's special counsel James Cole had completed his report on the case. The report will now be released on Jan. 16 instead of Feb. 4.
